summary.text: For Lemoine’s conjecture, each sufficiently large odd \(k\) is written as \(2\lfloor k/2\rfloor+1\) and the resulting representation is reordered, while the finitely many smaller odd cases are checked explicitly. For twin primes, assuming only finitely many eligible \(p\), the Chinese remainder theorem constructs a large odd target forcing the prime \(q\) in its representation to be divisible by a strictly smaller prime; hence there are infinitely many eligible \(p\), whose injective images under \(p\mapsto\operatorname{prime}(p+2)\) form infinitely many twin-prime pairs.

full_proof.text:
Let \(\pi_j\) denote the \(j\)-th prime when primes are indexed starting at \(0\), so
\[
\pi_0=2,\quad \pi_1=3,\quad \pi_2=5,\ldots.
\]
Thus the expression \(\operatorname{prime}(p+2)\), with the usual one-based indexing of primes, is \(\pi_{p+1}\).

Assume part (ii) of the A236566 conjecture in the following precise form:

> For every natural number \(n>30\), there are primes \(p,q\) such that \(\pi_{p+1}+2\) is also prime and
> \[
> 2n+1=2p+q.
> \tag{1}
> \]

We prove separately that this assumption implies Lemoine’s conjecture and the twin prime conjecture.

## 1. Lemoine’s conjecture

Lemoine’s conjecture says that every odd natural number \(k>5\) can be expressed as
\[
k=P+2Q
\]
with both \(P\) and \(Q\) prime.

Let \(k>5\) be odd. First suppose that \(k>61\). Since \(k\) is odd, if
\[
n=\left\lfloor\frac{k}{2}\right\rfloor,
\]
then
\[
k=2n+1.
\]
The inequality \(k>61\) implies \(n>30\). Applying the assumed part (ii) to this \(n\), we obtain primes \(p,q\) satisfying (1). Therefore
\[
k=2p+q=q+2p.
\]
This is a Lemoine representation, with \(P=q\) and \(Q=p\). Notice that the extra assertion that \(\pi_{p+1}+2\) is prime is not needed for this part of the argument.

It remains to deal with the odd integers \(k\) satisfying \(5<k\le 61\). The following table gives, for each such \(k\), primes \(P,Q\) with \(k=P+2Q\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|c@{\qquad}c|c@{\qquad}c|c}
 k&(P,Q)& &k&(P,Q)&\\ \hline
 7 &(3,2)&& 9 &(5,2)&\\
 11&(7,2)&&13&(7,3)&\\
 15&(11,2)&&17&(13,2)&\\
 19&(13,3)&&21&(17,2)&\\
 23&(19,2)&&25&(19,3)&\\
 27&(23,2)&&29&(23,3)&\\
 31&(17,7)&&33&(29,2)&\\
 35&(31,2)&&37&(31,3)&\\
 39&(29,5)&&41&(37,2)&\\
 43&(37,3)&&45&(41,2)&\\
 47&(43,2)&&49&(43,3)&\\
 51&(47,2)&&53&(47,3)&\\
 55&(41,7)&&57&(53,2)&\\
 59&(53,3)&&61&(47,7)&
\end{array}
\]
Every number occurring in a pair in the table is prime, and direct substitution verifies each equality. This covers all odd \(k>5\) not covered by the preceding argument. Hence Lemoine’s conjecture follows.

## 2. Infinitely many primes satisfying the A236566 side condition

Define
\[
S=\{p\in\mathbb N: p\text{ is prime and }\pi_{p+1}+2\text{ is prime}\}.
\]
We first prove that \(S\) is infinite.

Suppose, for a contradiction, that \(S\) is finite. For each \(p\in S\), define
\[
\ell_p=\pi_{p+2}.
\]
Each \(\ell_p\) is prime. Moreover, \(\ell_p>2\), because its index \(p+2\) is at least \(2\), and the prime at index \(2\) is \(5\). If \(p,p'\in S\) are distinct, then \(p+2\ne p'+2\); since the sequence of primes is strictly increasing, \(\ell_p\ne\ell_{p'}\). Consequently, the numbers
\[
2,\qquad \ell_p\quad(p\in S)
\]
are pairwise coprime: they are distinct primes, with every \(\ell_p\) odd.

The Chinese remainder theorem therefore supplies a natural number \(r\) simultaneously satisfying
\[
r\equiv 1\pmod 2
\tag{2}
\]
and
\[
r\equiv 2p\pmod{\ell_p}
\qquad\text{for every }p\in S.
\tag{3}
\]
Set
\[
P=2\prod_{p\in S}\ell_p.
\]
This is positive and divisible by every modulus used above. Hence every number of the form \(r+KP\) satisfies exactly the same congruences (2) and (3), for any natural number \(K\).

We now choose such a number large enough for two purposes: it must exceed \(61\), and it must be larger than \(2p+\ell_p\) for every \(p\in S\). To make this explicit, put
\[
B=\sum_{p\in S}(2p+\ell_p),\qquad K=B+100,
\]
and define
\[
M=r+KP.
\]
Since \(P\ge 1\), we have
\[
M\ge K=B+100>61.
\tag{4}
\]
Also, for every \(p\in S\), all summands defining \(B\) are nonnegative, so
\[
2p+\ell_p\le B<M.
\tag{5}
\]
Because \(P\) is divisible by \(2\) and by every \(\ell_p\), the defining congruences for \(r\) give
\[
M\equiv1\pmod2
\tag{6}
\]
and
\[
M\equiv2p\pmod{\ell_p}
\qquad(p\in S).
\tag{7}
\]
In particular, \(M\) is odd. Let
\[
n=\left\lfloor\frac M2\right\rfloor.
\]
From oddness we have
\[
M=2n+1,
\tag{8}
\]
and from \(M>61\) we obtain \(n>30\).

Apply part (ii) of the A236566 conjecture to this \(n\). It gives primes \(p,q\) such that \(\pi_{p+1}+2\) is prime and
\[
2n+1=2p+q.
\]
By (8), this says
\[
M=2p+q.
\tag{9}
\]
The primality of \(p\) and of \(\pi_{p+1}+2\) means precisely that \(p\in S\). We may therefore use congruence (7) for this particular \(p\). It yields
\[
M\equiv2p\pmod{\ell_p},
\]
so \(\ell_p\) divides \(M-2p\). Equation (9) gives \(M-2p=q\), and hence
\[
\ell_p\mid q.
\tag{10}
\]
On the other hand, inequality (5), applied to this \(p\), gives
\[
2p+\ell_p<M=2p+q,
\]
and therefore
\[
\ell_p<q.
\tag{11}
\]
But \(\ell_p\) is a prime greater than \(2\), so in particular \(1<\ell_p\). Equations (10) and (11) say that the prime number \(q\) has a divisor \(\ell_p\) strictly between \(1\) and \(q\), which is impossible. This contradiction proves that \(S\) is infinite.

## 3. From the infinite set \(S\) to infinitely many twin primes

Consider the map
\[
f:S\longrightarrow\mathbb N,\qquad f(p)=\pi_{p+1}.
\]
The sequence \(j\mapsto\pi_j\) is strictly increasing. Thus if
\[
f(p)=f(p'),

a strict monotonicity gives \(p+1=p'+1\), hence \(p=p'\). Therefore \(f\) is injective on \(S\). Since \(S\) is infinite, its image
\[
f(S)=\{\pi_{p+1}:p\in S\}
\]
is infinite as well.

For every \(p\in S\), the number \(\pi_{p+1}\) is prime by definition of the prime sequence, and \(\pi_{p+1}+2\) is prime by the defining property of \(S\). Hence every element \(r=f(p)\) of \(f(S)\) satisfies
\[
r\text{ prime},\qquad r+2\text{ prime}.
\]
Thus \(f(S)\) is an infinite subset of
\[
\{r\in\mathbb N:r\text{ and }r+2\text{ are prime}\}.
\]
The latter set is therefore infinite. This is exactly the twin prime conjecture.

We have proved from part (ii) of the A236566 conjecture both Lemoine’s conjecture and the twin prime conjecture.
